## Findings by module

### investing-2

- **confirmed** (ch-018.txt): Total return = dividend yield + capital gain yield, both divided by the starting price; a falling price can still give a positive total return thanks to dividends. Matches the course's total-return lesson.
- **confirmed** (ch-010.txt): Compound growth: future value = present value x (1 + r)^n; interest on interest (1,000 at 4% gives 1,040 then 1,081.60, the extra 1.60 being interest on interest); growth accelerates with time and with rate. Matches the course compounding lesson and formula.
- **confirmed** (ch-010.txt): Solving backwards: the same formula finds the years needed (15,000 to 25,000 at 6% takes 8.77 years) or the rate needed (15,000 to 25,000 in 8.5 years needs 6.194% a year); present value is always below future value when rates are positive. Matches the course's working-backwards example. OpenStax warns any calculator is only a tool: check that answers make sense.
- **refined** (ch-018.txt): OpenStax names the two averages: the geometric average (compounded annual return, what you actually earned per year) is always lower than the arithmetic average unless returns are identical; +50% then -50% gives 0% arithmetic but turns 100 into 75, in either order. Both are correct but answer different questions: geometric for growth over a period, arithmetic for a typical single year. The course calls the simple average misleading; refine to say it answers a different question.
- **refined** (ch-010.txt): The rule of 72 is a sourced textbook shortcut, not only our arithmetic: OpenStax gives years to double = 72 / rate (9% doubles in 8 years, 6% in 12; doubling in 5 years needs 14.4%). The course labels it a rule of thumb, not a sourced standard; it can now cite OpenStax.
- **extended** (ch-018.txt): Annualising: a holding-period return converts to an effective annual rate by (1 + HPR)^(1/years) - 1; the result equals the time-value-of-money rate. Example: Delta Air Lines 11.19 to 40.21 over 10 years is 259.34% total, 13.65% a year, though yearly returns ranged from -35.79% to +132.61% and four years were negative.
- **extended** (ch-010.txt): Why money now is worth more than money later: it can earn a return meanwhile, any promise of future payment carries default risk, and people naturally prefer to consume now, so saving must be rewarded. Higher promised rates usually carry more risk; only government securities are near-guaranteed. Echoes Fisher's impatience and opportunity.
- **extended** (ch-010.txt): Compounding frequency: the more often interest is credited, the larger the future value (1,000 at 6%: 1,060.00 annually, about 1,061.36 quarterly, 1,061.67 monthly); small on small sums, large on large sums over long periods. Discounting is compounding run backwards: 1,000 due in 30 years at 5% is worth 231.38 today.

### investing-3

- **extended** (ch-018.txt): Volatility is measured by the standard deviation of yearly returns. If returns were normally distributed, about two years in three fall within one standard deviation of the average, a loss worse than one SD below happens about one year in six. CVS 2011-2020: average 11.11%, SD 21.56%, so roughly -10.45% to +32.67% in two years of three. Gives the course a named measure for swings.
- **extended** (ch-018.txt): Risk premium, US 1928-2020: S&P 500 average return 11.64% a year (SD 19.49%, 25 negative years) against 3.36% for 3-month Treasury bills (SD 3.0%, never negative). The extra return is the reward for bearing risk; money needed soon belongs in the low-risk asset. US data, nominal, arithmetic averages (Damodaran).
- **extended** (ch-015.txt): Default-free government bonds still swing in price with interest rates: US Treasury bond total returns ranged from +32.81% (1982) to -8.25% (1999), averaging 10.21% in 1980-1999, and from +20.10% (2008) to -11.12% (2009) in 2000-2020. Safe from default is not the same as safe from loss.
- **extended** (ch-015.txt): Equity markets have earned negative annual returns about 25% of the time, far more often than bonds or money-market assets; stockholders bear more risk and on average receive higher returns. Annual S&P 500 returns 1928-2020 roughly follow a bell curve, which is why standard deviation is used as the risk measure.
- **extended** (ch-014.txt): Efficient market hypothesis (weak, semi-strong, strong forms): in a weak-form efficient market prices already reflect past prices and volume, so charting past prices (technical analysis) cannot reliably beat the market. Modern descendant of Bachelier's random-walk idea; believers hold it is pointless to hunt for undervalued shares or predict trends. (The text as printed defines only the weak form in the body; the summary names all three.)
- **extended** (ch-006.txt): US business cycles: contractions have averaged about 17 months and expansions about 41 months, a typical cycle about 4.5 years, but lengths vary widely (128-month expansion to February 2020; the 1929 to 1933 contraction lasted 43 months). Recessions are normal and recurring, which a stress test should assume.
- **extended** (ch-010.txt): No expected return is guaranteed: putting 1,000 into a favourite company expected to return 5% a year means accepting the risk of losing some or all of it in exchange for a chance to beat inflation. Risk and return together are why a dollar risked should earn more than a dollar kept safe. Opportunity cost: every choice, including doing nothing, gives up an alternative.
- **extended** (ch-013.txt): Bond risks beyond default: credit risk, liquidity risk, duration risk (the higher a bond's duration, the more its price moves for each 1% change in rates) and inflation eroding fixed payments. Yield to maturity is the market's return for holding to maturity at today's price; coupon above yield means a premium price, below means a discount. A normal yield curve slopes up; an inverted one (short rates above long) has preceded US recessions, including the inversion of March 2019 before the 2020 recession.

### investing-4

- **confirmed** (ch-018.txt): A portfolio's average return is the weighted average of its holdings' returns, but its standard deviation is lower than the weighted average of their SDs (equal four-stock example: 7.10% monthly, below every single stock) because returns are not perfectly correlated. Matches the course's Markowitz lesson.
- **extended** (ch-018.txt): Single shares are highly volatile even for established firms: 2011-2020 SDs of 51.90% (Delta), 49.84% (Southwest), 18.18% (ExxonMobil), 21.56% (CVS); company news such as a product recall can move a price about 15% in a day. Diversification means owning many holdings so one failure does not take all the money.
- **extended** (ch-018.txt): Correlation decides how much diversification helps: two airlines (correlation 0.87) cut Delta's SD only from 51.90% to 49.11%, while an airline plus an oil company (correlation 0.35) cut it to 30.43%; stocks in the same industry move together. Good worked numbers for the Markowitz lesson.
- **extended** (ch-018.txt): Firm-specific (unsystematic) risk can be diversified away; systematic (market) risk from interest rates, geopolitics, storms and pandemics cannot. Risk falls quickly from one stock to two or three, then each extra stock helps less (Statman 1987); 15 highly correlated stocks diversify less than 10 less correlated ones; about a dozen stocks gives reasonable diversification for an average investor.
- **extended** (ch-015.txt): US asset classes 1981-2020, arithmetic averages: large company stocks 12.64% (SD 16.06%), Baa corporate bonds 10.34% (7.67%), 10-year Treasuries 8.21% (9.92%), T-bills 3.94% (3.39%), inflation 2.93%. Advisers stress asset allocation first and stock picking second; 100 in 1928 grew far more in large company shares than in long government bonds. Small company shares returned more with more variability (142.9% in 1933, -58.0% in 1937).
- **extended** (ch-015.txt): US shares have been among the best-performing markets since 1900 (only Australia higher over 121 years, per Dimson, Marsh and Staunton); other established markets did not beat the US but offer diversification, and emerging markets carry the greatest return potential and risk of loss. Caution for a UK investor: US history is one fortunate market, not a guarantee (survivorship).
- **extended** (ch-006.txt): Currency risk: an exchange rate is the price of one currency in another, set by supply and demand; when the home currency appreciates, foreign receipts buy less of it. Our application: a UK investor in an overseas fund gains or loses on the exchange rate as well as the shares, a risk diversifying abroad adds. Price levels show how much inflation differs by country: with 1970 = 100, the 2020 CPI was 666.6 in the US, 302.3 in Switzerland and 331.8 in Japan.
- **extended** (ch-013.txt): Bond ladder: split money across bonds maturing at regular intervals (for example one to ten years) and replace each as it matures; shorter rungs give stability, longer rungs higher yield, and the mix carries less rate risk than long bonds alone. Selling a bond before maturity can give a gain or loss: a 7% bond must fall in price until it yields the 10% now on offer.

### investing-5

- **extended** (ch-018.txt): An advertised average return is meaningless without its risk: the Sharpe ratio divides excess return over the risk-free rate by the standard deviation; Jensen's alpha compares a fund with what its market risk (beta) should have earned. A higher-return manager can be the worse one once risk is counted. Beta: 1 moves with the market, 2 moves twice as much; sources report different betas for the same stock.
- **extended** (ch-015.txt): An ETF is a basket of securities that trades on an exchange like a single share, letting an investor own a broad portfolio in one transaction (example: a fund of 3 to 7 year government bonds).
- **note** (ch-015.txt): Even a celebrated active manager (Bill Gross, the bond king) failed to beat bond fund averages in his later career; OpenStax presents this as efficient-market odds catching up. Illustrates why past star performance does not persist.

### investing-1

- **confirmed** (ch-014.txt): Shares promise no cash flows: no maturity, no face value, dividends only if the board declares them and subject to change, so shares are riskier than bonds. Matches the course's description of shares as ownership with uncertain returns.
- **confirmed** (ch-006.txt): Real interest rate = nominal rate minus inflation (OpenStax's simple form): 6% nominal with 2% inflation leaves 4% real; the real rate is the true reward for delaying spending and the true cost of borrowing (1980: 15% nominal less 12% inflation = 3% real). Matches the course's nominal-versus-real teaching.
- **refined** (ch-010.txt): The Fisher effect, named for Irving Fisher: (1 + nominal) = (1 + real) x (1 + expected inflation); a 6% real return with 2% inflation needs 8.12% nominal. Subtracting inflation from the nominal rate is an approximation; the exact real return on 5% nominal with 3% inflation is 1.05 / 1.03 - 1 = 1.94% (our arithmetic). The course says about 2%; add the exact form and name Fisher, who is a course lecturer.
- **extended** (ch-015.txt): Asset classes in order of claim: bonds have contractual interest and repayment of face value at maturity; preferred shares rank above common but below bonds; common shareholders are residual claimants with no contract guaranteeing dividends or resale price, so their cash flows are more uncertain. Inflation-linked government bonds (US TIPS) adjust principal with the consumer price index. Bond ratings run from AAA (investment grade) down through BBB to BB and below (junk, high risk).
- **extended** (ch-015.txt): Inflation in practice: expected inflation is built into interest rates; when actual inflation beats it, fixed-rate lenders lose and borrowers gain, so inflation redistributes wealth. Prices do not rise evenly: US CPI 1980-2020 averaged 2.90% a year while tuition rose 6.49% and rent 3.67%; a basket costing 100 in 1984 cost about 260 by 2020 at only 2.55% a year. Your own inflation depends on what you buy.
- **extended** (ch-014.txt): A share's price is the present value of the dividend stream a buyer will receive; each buyer buys the remaining stream. Preferred shares pay fixed dividends ahead of ordinary shareholders, often cumulative, usually without votes, and behave more like bonds. Models are only as good as their inputs: garbage in, garbage out.
- **extended** (ch-006.txt): How inflation is measured: the consumer price index tracks the cost of a fixed basket of goods and services in weighted categories (food, housing, clothing, transport, medical care, recreation, education and communication, other); core inflation excludes volatile food and energy prices. The basket goes out of date as habits change and people substitute cheaper goods, so the index is an approximation. US example: 100 dollars in 1913 had the purchasing power of 2,699.20 in 2021. (UK equivalent is the ONS CPI; check UK figures before quoting.)
- **extended** (ch-006.txt): Interest is the rental price of money set by savers and borrowers; riskier borrowers pay a credit-risk premium, which is why unsecured credit card rates sit far above government and prime business rates (no collateral). Supports clearing expensive debt before investing (our inference: no investment reliably beats a high card rate).
- **extended** (ch-010.txt): Negative real rates erode cash: holding 1,000 for a year at a real rate of -3.65% loses 36.50 of purchasing power. If savings grow faster than inflation, purchasing power rises; if slower, it falls. Low rates push savers out of cash and short government debt.
- **extended** (ch-010.txt): Debt before investing: OpenStax says that rather than investing you should probably pay down 24% APR credit card debt first, since it costs more than an investment account is likely to earn; by the rule of 72 an unpaid 24% balance doubles in about 3 years. Prices rising at 3% instead of 2% double in 24 years instead of 36. Supports the course's safety-net-first order with a sourced debt rule.
- **extended** (ch-013.txt): A bond is a loan to the issuer: fixed coupons plus repayment of face value at maturity. Bond prices move opposite to interest rates (the seesaw): when rates rise, existing fixed-rate bonds fall in value, and the lower the coupon, the bigger the price swing (zero-coupon bonds swing most); floating-rate bonds avoid this. Government bills are safest and pay least; corporate bonds pay more for credit risk, junk bonds most. Bonds add stability and income with less volatility than shares.

### investing-6

- **extended** (ch-015.txt): Buying new issues (IPOs) straight after listing has historically lost money relative to the market: Malkiel, cited by OpenStax, reports IPOs underperforming by about 4% a year; IPO costs run 5% to 8% of the issue. Supports a caution against hot new listings in the speculation lesson.
- **extended** (ch-015.txt): Market timing: 10,000 in an S&P 500 index fund from 1980 to mid-2020 grew to 697,421; missing the 5 best days cut it to 432,411 and missing the 10 best to 313,377. Supports the discipline lesson against jumping in and out.
- **extended** (ch-014.txt): Valuation tools behind a margin of safety: a share's intrinsic value can be estimated as the present value of its expected future dividends (dividend discount model; Gordon growth model price = next dividend / (required return - growth)), and the P/E ratio shows how much the market pays per unit of earnings. OpenStax stresses that any single ratio means little on its own; compare with the company's history and its industry, and every model rests on assumptions that may fail.
- **extended** (ch-014.txt): Valuation estimates are fragile: OpenStax says a single percentage point change in the assumed growth rate or required return can move a dividend-model fair price by as much as 10 to 20%, and the model fails for firms that pay no dividends (Berkshire, Amazon, Google reinvest instead). A strong practical case for Graham's margin of safety: buy well below your estimate because the estimate is uncertain.
- **extended** (ch-013.txt): Ratings are judgements, not guarantees: Enron's bonds were rated investment grade about two months before its December 2001 bankruptcy, cut to junk only on 28 November 2001 after restated accounts; in 2001, 11% of US junk bond issues defaulted. Investment grade is BBB/Baa or above; below is speculative. Supports the course point that a label or authorisation is not protection.
- **note** (ch-015.txt): SPACs (blank-cheque companies) raise money before choosing a target; of 89 completed SPAC mergers 2015-July 2020, shares averaged a loss of 18.8% (median -36.1%) against an average +37.2% after-market return for traditional IPOs (Renaissance Capital).
- **note** (ch-015.txt): Buffett, a follower of Graham, avoided dot-com shares he could not understand and lagged until the bubble burst; he stresses long holding periods. Illustrates Graham's method surviving a speculative boom.
